label: bm-lay-analogies
topic: Plain-language explanations that are also correct
summary: Nine plain-language explanations were written, each with a 3-6 sentence paragraph, an everyday comparison, a note on where the comparison breaks, a one-line common wrong idea and its source; all quoted evidence was checked word for word against the pages and PDFs fetched in this run (quote_check.json; a doctored control quote correctly fails). Topics: pine cone opening (Reyssat and Mahadevan 2009: opens dry, closes wet, dead tissue works, active cells change length about 10 % between dry and saturated air), bilayer as bimetal strip, what a Lean law is, proof versus simulation, why a ceiling rules out designs, what 0.7 % water uptake means, why thin is faster, why a stiffer partner does not curl more, and why Elastic 50A swells in alcohol but not water. New beyond the earlier files: (1) the 3/2 ceiling is readable in the 1863 bimetal formula, kappa = 3/(2a) x mismatch/h with a = 1 + (square) >= 1, which I showed equals the project coefficient to 7e-16 over 200,000 random cases, so a layperson can see the ceiling without Lean; Holstov 2015 had already plotted it, so it is not a new discovery, only a newly proved one. (2) I re-ran the Lean check (5 theorems, 0 errors, 0 sorryAx) and two false versions (ceiling 7/5), which Lean refuses. (3) 0.7 % water uptake is 7 mg per gram, about a sixth of a drop for a 1.2 g cube; I estimate 0.09-0.28 % length change, and a bilayer magnifies a stretch by 0.75 L/h = 37.5 (tip moves 1.3-4.2 mm on a 40 mm, 0.8 mm strip at best). (4) CONTRADICTION: the earlier claim that every current Formlabs SLA resin gains under 1 % in water is false for Flexible 80A V2 (+8 % mass in 1 day, ASTM D471 slab); the 0.7 % is the cube test on a differently named resin row; the sibling file bm-resin-water-uptake-data.json reached the same correction and I confirm it from the PDF. (5) The 39 % isopropanol figure is Elastic 50A V2 (V1 is 25.6 %), confirmed against Rigid 10K <0.1 %. (6) The thin-is-faster rule is a 4x law only ideally; pine cones measure exponents 1.3-1.5, and bimetal heat is 19 million times faster than water in dense resin, which is where the bimetal analogy fails most. No measured humid-air swelling or water diffusivity exists for any Formlabs resin; all such figures here are labelled estimates.
lay_summary: A pine cone is made of two layers stuck together. When the air dries out, one layer shrinks and the other does not, so each scale bends open. Printed plastic can do the same thing if two layers swell by different amounts, but plastic swells far less than a pine cone does. We checked, with a computer program that accepts only complete proofs, that a two-layer strip can never curl tighter than a fixed limit set by its thickness and how much it swells. That means we can rule out some shapes on paper before wasting a print. Thin strips respond faster, but the time falls with the square of the thickness, so a strip half as thick is about four times quicker in theory and about two and a half times in real cones.

glossary.plain: Two layers stuck face to face, as in the scale of a pine cone.
Two metals bonded together that bend when heated because they expand by different amounts.
How much more one layer lengthens than the other, as a fraction of its length.
How sharply a strip bends: one divided by the radius of the circle it follows.
A limit that no choice of layers can beat; here, 1.5 times the mismatch divided by the strip's thickness.
A computer program that checks mathematical proofs step by step and refuses incomplete ones.
A proof covers every case at once; a simulation only checks the cases it tries.
How much heavier a part gets when it absorbs water, as a percent of its starting weight.
Slow spreading of water into a material; D says how fast, in square metres per second.
How hard a material pushes back when you stretch or bend it.
A material that changes shape when humidity changes.
Liquid plastic hardened by light in a printer (Form 4 uses this).

findings.claim: Pine cones open when dried and close when wetted.
findings.evidence_quote: Using the pine cone as an example that opens when dried and closes when wet

findings.claim: Fallen pine cones are dead and still open and close repeatedly with humidity, so no living process is needed.
findings.evidence_quote: But when dead fallen dry cones are moved into a humid environment, they close and open again when dried, an experiment that may be repeated many times.

findings.claim: The cone scale works through a two-layer structure: an active outer layer of long thick-walled cells that lengthen when humid and shorten when dry, and an inner passive layer that responds much less.
findings.evidence_quote: closely packed long parallel thick-walled cells respond by expanding longitudinally when exposed to humidity

findings.claim: Reyssat and Mahadevan state the scale tissue behaves like a bimetallic strip, with humidity replacing temperature.
findings.value: bimetal analogy used by the cone researchers
findings.evidence_quote: Consequently, the tissue behaves like a thermally actuated bimetallic strip that curves in response to temperature changes because of the differential expansion of the constituent strips that are glued together.

findings.claim: Measured hygrometric expansion coefficient of the cone's active cells is 0.001 per percent relative humidity; over 0 to 100 percent RH that is a length change of about 10 percent (own multiplication).
findings.evidence_quote: the hygrometric expansion coefficient of the cells that characterizes the strain per relative humidity α = 0.001 ± 0.0001

findings.claim: The authors expect a curvature change of about 1.3 per cm for a 1 mm thick scale going from zero to saturated humidity, which gives a scale-opening angle of roughly 75 degrees.
findings.evidence_quote: Δκ ∼ 1.3 cm −1 (for h ∼ 1 mm and Δϕ = 100, i.e. relative humidity changing from zero to saturation)

findings.claim: Cone researchers built a paper-and-plastic copy that curls on drying and straightens on wetting (everyday model of the cone).
findings.evidence_quote: we also build bilayer hygromorphs of a thin layer of plastic attached to paper which curl upon drying and straighten on wetting

findings.claim: A bimetal strip converts temperature change into mechanical displacement, and the sideways displacement is much larger than the lengthways expansion of either metal (the bend amplifies a small stretch).
findings.evidence_quote: The sideways displacement of the strip is much larger than the small lengthways expansion in either of the two metals.

findings.claim: The classical (1863, Villarceau) bimetal curvature formula is kappa = 3/(2a) x (mismatch strain)/h with a = 1 + (E1 h1^2 - E2 h2^2)^2 / (4 E1 h1 E2 h2 h^2). Because a is 1 plus a square, a >= 1, so kappa <= 1.5 x mismatch / h, with equality when E1 h1^2 = E2 h2^2. This is the project's 3/2 ceiling and its optimum m^2 n = 1 in older notation.

The project's coefficient f(m,n) equals 1.5/a of the Villarceau form to rounding error: largest absolute difference 6.7e-16 over 200,000 random thickness and stiffness pairs spanning four decades each.

CONTRADICTS the idea that the 3/2 ceiling is new: Holstov, Bridgens and Farmer (2015) plotted f(m,n) for many stiffness ratios and wrote that its maximum stays at 1.5. What the project adds is the kernel-checked proof and the closed-form optimum. (Confirms the sibling file bm-wood-cellulose-hygromorphs.json; also shows the ceiling is visible in an 1863 formula.)
findings.evidence_quote: Plotting f(m,n) for a wide range of possible stiffness ratios shows that the maximum value of the function remains constant at 1.5

findings.claim: Holstov et al. warn equal layer thickness costs response in their fibreglass-and-wood example: up to 60 percent. My recomputation with n=30 gives f(1,30)=0.545, a 63.7 percent loss against 1.5.
findings.evidence_quote: If the layers were of equal thickness, for the same overall thickness of the composite the response would be reduced by as much as 60%.

findings.claim: When one layer is infinitely stiffer than the other (stiffness ratio 0 or infinity) there is no bending; and at equal thickness the coefficient changes by less than 10 percent when the stiffness ratio varies from 0.3 to 3.5 (my calculation: 0.86 percent).
findings.value: f=0 at n->0 or inf; <10 % change n=0.3..3.5
findings.evidence_quote: In the limit where n is 0 or +∞, one of the layers is infinitely more rigid than the other, and f ( m,n ) = 0: no bending occurs.

findings.claim: With a stiffness ratio of 10 and equal thickness the coefficient is 0.9959, 66.4 percent of the 1.5 ceiling (a 34 percent loss); at the optimal thickness ratio m = n^-1/2 it is exactly 1.5 for every n tested (0.001 to 10000).

The Lean kernel check of HygromorphCeilingCheck.lean, re-run 2026-11-12 with the project's check.sh (toolchain leanprover/lean4:v4.35.0), reports errors=0, sorryAx=0, and five theorems each depending only on propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. The theorem bilayer_rules_out says any claimed curvature above 3/2 x mismatch / h cannot be reached.
findings.evidence_quote: theorem bilayer_rules_out (h m n Δε κ_claimed : ℝ) (hh : 0 < h) (hm : 0 < m) (hn : 0 < n)

findings.claim: Lean refuses a false version of the law: with the ceiling stated as 7/5 instead of 3/2 (value 1.4 instead of 1.5) Lean gives 'error: linarith failed to find a contradiction', and a version with a 'sorry' placeholder is listed as depending on sorryAx. A failure to prove is a refusal, not itself a disproof; the disproof of 7/5 is that the optimum gives exactly 3/2 (theorem bilayerCurvature_optimal).
findings.evidence_quote: error: linarith failed to find a contradiction

findings.claim: Lean's own documentation says an interactive prover requires every step to be justified down to basic axioms, in contrast to automated reasoning systems that can trade soundness for power.
findings.evidence_quote: every rule of inference and every step of a calculation has to be justified by appealing to prior definitions and theorems, all the way down to basic axioms and rules

findings.claim: Lean's documentation notes that verifying a real system requires first describing it in mathematical terms, so the proof covers the description, not the object (basis of the 'where the analogy breaks' note for E3).
findings.value: description step is outside the proof
findings.evidence_quote: formal verification requires describing hardware and software systems in mathematical terms

findings.claim: Sampling 2,000,000 random thickness and stiffness combinations (log-uniform, 1e-3 to 1e3) gave a maximum coefficient of 1.4999999999740508, never above 1.5, and the best sample had m^2 n close to 1; this is evidence, not proof.
Euler's polynomial n^2+n+41 gives a prime for each n from 0 to 39 (40 passes) and first fails at n=40 with 1681 = 41 x 41; a worked example of tests passing then failing.

Ceiling arithmetic R_min = h / (1.5 x mismatch): h=0.8 mm and 0.2 percent mismatch give R_min=266.7 mm; a 50 mm radius at h=0.8 mm needs at least 1.067 percent mismatch; at h=0.4 mm it needs 0.533 percent.
Formlabs' solvent table is a 24-hour weight-gain test on printed 1 cm cubes that were washed and post-cured: it is neither an equilibrium value nor a size change.
findings.evidence_quote: Formlabs measures resistance to solvents by observing, measuring, and weighing printed cubes (originally measuring 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm) before and after immersion in a solvent for 24 hours.

findings.claim: Confirms the earlier record: on the current Formlabs page Elastic 50A Resin V2 shows 39.2 percent in isopropyl alcohol and 0.7 percent in water; Rigid 10K shows <0.1 percent in both. Column order from the page header (Isopropyl Alcohol is the 10th solvent, Water the 18th).
Same row for Rigid 10K Resin (both IPA and water <0.1 percent).

Elastic 50A Resin V1 on the same page takes up 25.6 percent IPA and 2.3 percent water, so the '39 percent' belongs to V2 and V1 is the Formlabs resin with the highest water gain in that table among the rows read.

The row labelled plain 'Flexible 80A Resin' shows 0.7 percent in water and 11.7 percent in IPA (same 24 h cube test). This is the '0.7 percent' in the earlier record; the page does not state a version.

CONTRADICTS the earlier claim (spec-resin-chemistry.json) that every current Formlabs SLA resin gains under 1 percent mass in water. The Flexible 80A V2 data sheet (ASTM D471 full immersion) lists deionized water at 1 day: hardness -26 Shore A points, mass +8 percent, volume +3 percent; 1 week: mass +9 percent, volume +7 percent. Different resin version and method from the 0.7 percent cube; both are real. (Same correction was already made by the sibling file bm-resin-water-uptake-data.json; confirmed here from the PDF.)

Caution on the Flexible 80A V2 volume column: for isooctane the table gives +56 percent mass but +164 percent volume at 1 week, more than simple mass-additivity allows (about +90 to +100 percent using an assumed resin density 1.1 to 1.21 and isooctane density 0.69, both unverified background); for water volume (+3 %) is below mass-additivity (about +9 %). So strain derived from the volume column is uncertain; I use 0.12 percent length per percent mass only as a low-end figure.
Clear Resin V5 density is 1.21 g/cm3 (ASTM D792); used as a stand-in density for a printed Formlabs resin cube (about 1.2 g for 1 cm^3). Density of Elastic 50A and Flexible 80A was not read.
findings.evidence_quote: Density 1.21 g/cm3

findings.claim: A 0.7 percent uptake is 7 mg of water per gram of resin, about 8.5 mg in a 1.21 g cube; at 0.05 mL per drop (and 1 g/mL water, unverified background) that is 0.14 drop per gram and 0.17 drop per cube; 8 percent would be 80 mg per gram, 1.6 drops.
findings.evidence_quote: In this usage, a drop is typically considered to be approximately 0.05 mL.

findings.claim: Wikipedia itself warns a drop is not a fixed volume, which limits the drop comparison to an order of magnitude.
findings.evidence_quote: The volume of a drop is not well defined

findings.claim: Estimated length change for 0.7 percent mass gain: low 0.087 percent (using 0.124 percent length per percent mass from the Flexible 80A V2 1-day volume +3 %, cube-root) and high 0.282 percent (ideal volume mixing, resin density 1.21 / 3 = 0.40 per percent mass). On 40 mm that is 0.035 to 0.113 mm. Both are estimates; no measured strain exists for a Formlabs resin in the sources read.

At the ceiling with a perfectly passive partner, a 40 mm long, 0.8 mm thick strip with those mismatches reaches radius 616 to 189 mm and a tip deflection of 1.3 to 4.2 mm; tip deflection divided by elongation is about 0.75 L/h = 37.5 in both cases.

Reyssat and Mahadevan: with a diffusion constant of about 1e-9 m2/s and a 1 mm active layer, tau = h^2/D is about 1000 s; but the measured fits are drying 96 h_a^1.5 min and wetting 29 h_a^1.3 min (h_a in mm), so the real exponents are 1.5 and 1.3, not 2.
findings.evidence_quote: the shrinking (drying) time varies as τ d = 96 h a 1.5 min and the swelling (wetting) time varies as τ d = 29 h a 1.3 min (where h a is in mm)

findings.claim: Reyssat and Mahadevan's order-of-magnitude statement of the square law.
findings.evidence_quote: For molecular pores, D ∼ 10 −9 m 2 s −1 , the thickness of the active layer h a ∼ 1 mm and τ = h a 2 / D ∼ 1000 s

findings.claim: Doubling thickness multiplies the time by 4 in the ideal square law, by 2.83 for the measured pine drying exponent (1.5) and 2.46 for the wetting exponent (1.3).

Time to 90 percent of final water for a layer open on one face is 0.848 h^2/D (50 percent: 0.197, 99 percent: 1.78), from the Crank slab series, solved by bisection in calc.py (matches sibling file bm-diffusion-kinetics.json). For D = 1e-12 m2/s: 0.2 mm 9.4 h; 0.4 mm 37.7 h; 0.8 mm 150.8 h (6.3 days); 1.6 mm 603 h (25 days). For D = 1e-11: 0.94, 3.8, 15.1, 60.3 h. For D = 1e-9: 34 s, 2.3 min, 9 min, 36 min.

A water diffusion coefficient of 0.85e-12 m2/s was reported for 3D-printed PMMA dental resin (37 C, a non-Formlabs resin); the sibling file recomputed about 2.6e-13 from the same paper's medians. I found no measured water diffusivity for any Formlabs resin, so 1e-12 is an order of magnitude, and times could be about 3 times longer.
findings.evidence_quote: Diffusion coefficient was calculated and values as D = 1.02–1.15 × 10 −12 m 2 /s for milled and 0.85 × 10 −12 m 2 /s for printed materials were obtained.

findings.claim: Thermal diffusivity of AISI 1010 steel is 18.8 mm2/s and of nylon 0.09 mm2/s. Heat reaches 90 percent equilibrium across 1 mm of steel in 0.045 s (0.848 x 1^2 / 18.8), against about 9.8 days for water in a 1 mm dense resin at D=1e-12 m2/s: a ratio of 1.9e7 in diffusivity.
findings.evidence_quote: Steel , AISI 1010 (0.1% carbon) 18.8

findings.claim: Force and stroke trade against thickness: curvature falls as 1/h while blocking force rises roughly as h^2 (project record, own beam-theory derivation in spec-bilayer-physics.json, not re-derived here), so thin is faster but weaker.

Project record, not re-derived here: six beech bilayers from the ETH dataset reach kappa x h / mismatch of 1.35, 1.50, 1.53, 1.36, 1.04, 0.91; the 1.53 uses nominal swelling coefficients, so it signals uncertainty, not a counter-example to the ceiling.

Readability check of the nine explanation paragraphs (Flesch-Kincaid grade, own implementation with a syllable heuristic) is reported in readability.json; none exceeded 11 (range 6.3 to 10.6, mean 9.4); this is a rough machine estimate, not a reader test.

key_claims.claim: A pine-cone scale is a two-layer structure that opens when dried and closes when wetted, and dead fallen cones keep doing this, so the explanation needs no living process.
key_claims.evidence_quote: But when dead fallen dry cones are moved into a humid environment, they close and open again when dried, an experiment that may be repeated many times.

key_claims.claim: The curl ceiling kappa <= 1.5 x mismatch / h is both Lean-checked (this run: 5 theorems, 0 errors, 0 sorryAx) and visible in the classical 1863 bimetal formula, where kappa = 3/(2a) x mismatch/h and a = 1 + a square >= 1; it is not new (Holstov 2015 plotted it) but its proof is.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Plotting f(m,n) for a wide range of possible stiffness ratios shows that the maximum value of the function remains constant at 1.5

key_claims.claim: Formlabs' 0.7 % is a 24-hour weight gain of a 1 cm cube for the rows Flexible 80A and Elastic 50A V2, not an equilibrium value and not a size change; Flexible 80A V2 gains +8 % mass in one day by another method, so no single 'water uptake of Formlabs resins' exists.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Formlabs measures resistance to solvents by observing, measuring, and weighing printed cubes (originally measuring 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm) before and after immersion in a solvent for 24 hours.

key_claims.claim: Diffusion time scales as thickness squared in the ideal case (4x for double thickness), but pine-cone data give exponents 1.5 (drying) and 1.3 (wetting), so real strips are 2.5 to 4 times faster when half as thick.
key_claims.evidence_quote: the shrinking (drying) time varies as τ d = 96 h a 1.5 min and the swelling (wetting) time varies as τ d = 29 h a 1.3 min (where h a is in mm)

table.name: E1-pine-cone: Why a pine cone opens when it dries
table.fields: explanation=Each scale of a pine cone is two layers stuck together. The outer layer is made of long, thick-walled cells that get longer when they take up moisture and shorter when they dry. The inner layer hardly changes size. When the air dries, the outer layer shrinks and the inner one does not, so the scale is forced to curve outward and the cone opens. When the cone gets wet, the outer layer lengthens again and the scales close. Fallen cones are dead wood, so no living cell is doing the work: it is purely swelling and shrinking of dry material. | everyday_comparison=A strip of plastic tape stuck along one side of a sheet of paper: the paper takes up and loses moisture, the tape does not, and the sheet curls. | where_it_breaks=The paper-and-plastic version was built by the cone researchers as a copy (it curls on drying and straightens on wetting), so it is a fair model of the mechanism. It breaks on size and speed: the cone's cells change length by about 10 percent between dry and saturated air (0.001 per percent of relative humidity x 100 [calc]), far more than a stock printed resin manages (a few tenths of a percent), and the cone opens more slowly than it closes (drying time 96 h_a^1.5 min against wetting 29 h_a^1.3 min, h_a in mm). | common_wrong_idea=Wrong: the cone is alive and opens on purpose when it senses rain or warmth. Right: it opens when DRY and closes when WET, and it does so even when dead. | sentences=6

table.name: E2-bilayer-bimetal: Why two layers that swell unequally bend, like a bimetal strip
table.fields: explanation=A bimetal strip is two metals bonded face to face that expand by different amounts when heated. The layer that wants to grow longer cannot slide past its partner, so the whole strip bends, with the longer-growing layer on the outside of the curve. A water-driven bilayer works the same way, except moisture instead of heat makes one layer change size. Only a difference in change is needed, so the second layer can simply stay put, as the inner layer of a pine-cone scale does. The bend is much larger than the tiny stretch that causes it, because a long thin strip turns a small length difference into a large sideways swing. The same equation, worked out by Timoshenko in 1925 for thermostats, is used for both. | everyday_comparison=Two runners on a curved running track: the runner in the outer lane has a longer path, so if two lanes are tied together the longer one must sit on the outside of the bend. A thermostat or dial thermometer is the real-world example. | where_it_breaks=The track picture gives the direction of the bend but not how much. The big break is speed: heat spreads through 1 mm of steel in about 0.05 s (thermal diffusivity 18.8 mm2/s [calc]), but water creeping into a dense resin (D about 1e-12 m2/s) needs about 10 days for the same 1 mm, roughly 19 million times slower [calc]. Also, in a thermostat both metals expand; in a hygromorph usually one layer does the swelling and the other is a passive partner. | common_wrong_idea=Wrong: one layer must grow while the other shrinks. Right: only a difference in change is needed; one layer can stay the same size. | sentences=6

table.name: E3-lean-law: What a 'law' in Lean is
table.fields: explanation=Lean is a computer program that checks mathematical proofs. A 'law' in this project is a statement typed into Lean, for example: for any two layers of any thickness and any stiffness, the curl per unit of swelling mismatch can never exceed 3/2 divided by the total thickness. Lean accepts the statement only if there is a chain of steps in which every step follows from earlier results, down to a few basic rules. If one step is missing, Lean refuses, and our check script also fails if a placeholder called 'sorry' was left in. On 12 Nov 2026 we ran the project's file: five theorems, no errors, no placeholders [calc: lean_check_out.txt]. | everyday_comparison=A strict referee who redoes every line of your arithmetic and will not accept 'it is obvious'. | where_it_breaks=A referee of the sums does not know whether you wrote down the right problem. Lean checks the mathematics of the formula we typed in; it cannot check that the formula describes a real printed strip. The Lean file's formula was matched by us to two independent published forms (Reyssat 2009 and the 1863 form on Wikipedia, identical to 1e-15 over 200,000 random cases [calc]), but that match is a human check, not a Lean check. | common_wrong_idea=Wrong: 'checked by Lean' means the physical strip is guaranteed to behave that way. Right: it guarantees the maths of the model; the real strip must also meet the model's assumptions (thin, elastic, small bend, well-bonded layers). | sentences=5

table.name: E4-proof-vs-simulation: Why a proof differs from a simulation
table.fields: explanation=A simulation tries particular cases and reports what happened. A proof shows something is true for every case at once, including ones nobody tried. We sampled 2 million random layer combinations and the largest curl coefficient found was 1.49999999997, never above 1.5 [calc]. That is strong evidence, but it is not a guarantee. The Lean proof reduces to the fact that a squared number is never negative, so no combination can beat 1.5. Tests can pass for a long time and then fail: the formula n x n + n + 41 gives a prime number for every n from 0 to 39 and fails at n = 40, where it gives 1681 = 41 x 41 [calc]. | everyday_comparison=Trying a million keys in a lock versus showing from the lock's design that no key of this shape can open it. | where_it_breaks=A proof only speaks about the model; a simulation or a real print can reveal that the model itself is wrong, which no proof can. For the strip, the published bilayer data are consistent with the proved ceiling (six beech bilayers peak at 1.50-1.53 against 1.5 [rec]) and the 1.53 slightly above the bound shows measurement uncertainty, not a broken proof. | common_wrong_idea=Wrong: a plot or simulation that never crosses the limit has proved the limit. Right: Holstov et al. (2015) plotted the maximum as 1.5 for many stiffness ratios; the Lean proof is what turns the observation into a certainty. | sentences=6
table.source: Holstov 2015 (doi 10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2015.08.136; open copy https://doi.org/10.25405/ncl.34238076) ; own calculation calc.py ; HygromorphCeilingCheck.lean

table.name: E5-ceiling-rules-out: Why a ceiling on curl lets a design be ruled out before printing
table.fields: explanation=The proven ceiling says the curl of a two-layer strip, measured as 1/radius, can never exceed 1.5 times the swelling mismatch divided by the total thickness, however the layers are chosen. So if you know how much your materials can swell, you can work out the tightest possible curl before printing anything. A 0.8 mm strip whose layers differ in swelling by 0.2 percent can never curl tighter than a circle of radius 267 mm, a circle about half a metre wide [calc]. To curl to a 50 mm radius the same strip needs at least 1.07 percent mismatch [calc]. A design asking for more is ruled out on paper, which saves a print, a cure and a week of soaking. | everyday_comparison=A fuel tank and the best possible mileage: no engine can drive farther than tank size times the best mileage physics allows, so you can rule out a 2,000 km trip on 10 litres before building the car. | where_it_breaks=The ceiling is an upper bound for an idealised two-layer strip, not a promise: real strips reach less (the six beech bilayers scored 0.91 to 1.53 of the 1.5 limit [rec]; a cellulose-acetate film reached 65 percent of it [rec]). It does not cover other structures such as lattices, gradients, or wide plates that curve in two directions, and it rests on the swelling mismatch being known, which for Formlabs resins nobody has measured. | common_wrong_idea=Wrong: you must print and test to learn whether a shape is possible, or that the 3/2 ceiling is a new discovery. Right: with a known swelling mismatch, a lower limit on the radius is arithmetic; the ceiling itself was already seen in 2015 and its closed form follows from a 1863 formula. | sentences=5

table.name: E6-water-uptake-0.7pct: What a water uptake of 0.7 percent means
table.fields: explanation=Water uptake of 0.7 percent means 100 g of plastic gained 0.7 g of water. A 1 cm cube of printed resin weighs about 1.2 g, so it takes in roughly 8 mg, less than a fifth of a drop [calc]. The water squeezes in between the plastic's molecules and makes the part slightly bigger, by our estimate 0.09 to 0.28 percent in length, about 0.04 to 0.11 mm along a 40 mm strip [calc]. Alone that is invisible, but a thin bilayer magnifies it about 37 times: the tip of a 40 mm long, 0.8 mm thick strip could move 1.3 to 4.2 mm at best [calc]. And 0.7 percent is Formlabs' 24-hour cube test, not the final amount, and it describes one resin: the Flexible 80A V2 data sheet reports +8 percent mass in one day. | everyday_comparison=A sixth of a drop of water inside a 1.2 g cube; or, scaled up, half a kilogram of water gained by a 70 kg person. | where_it_breaks=The drop sits on a surface in the picture, but the real water is inside the plastic. A 'drop' is not a fixed volume (about 0.05 mL by convention). Mass percent is not length percent: the conversion is 0.12 to 0.40 percent of length per percent of mass [calc], and we have no measured value for any Formlabs resin in humid air. | common_wrong_idea=Wrong: 0.7 percent is nothing, so the plastic cannot change shape (or is waterproof). Right: small swelling matters once a thin bilayer amplifies it, but it is also small: a 0.2 percent mismatch caps a 0.8 mm strip at a 267 mm radius. | sentences=5

table.name: E7-thin-is-faster: Why a thin strip is faster than a thick one
table.fields: explanation=Water spreads into plastic slowly, like ink spreading through still water, and the time it takes grows with the square of the distance it must travel. Make the layer twice as thick and, in the ideal case, it takes four times as long; make it half as thick and it takes a quarter. For a dense resin with a water diffusivity of about 1e-12 m2/s, a 0.2 mm layer reaches 90 percent of its final water in about 9 hours, 0.4 mm in about 38 hours, 0.8 mm in about 6 days, and 1.6 mm in about 25 days [calc]. A porous pine-cone layer is about a thousand times quicker (D near 1e-9 m2/s), so a 1 mm layer needs minutes to a couple of hours. The price of being thin is strength: the force a strip can push with falls roughly as the thickness squared [rec]. | everyday_comparison=Thin fries cook through much sooner than thick wedges, because heat also spreads by the same square-law. | where_it_breaks=Real objects are not ideal: for pine-cone scales Reyssat and Mahadevan measured exponents of 1.5 for drying and 1.3 for wetting, not 2, so doubling thickness slows the cone by 2.5 to 2.8 times, not 4 [calc]. Cooking adds surface effects and evaporation, so the fries comparison is only the same family of mathematics, and was not tested here. The 1e-12 diffusivity is an order of magnitude from printed dental resin (0.85e-12 m2/s); no value for a Formlabs resin has been measured, so the times could be 3 times longer or shorter. | common_wrong_idea=Wrong: half as thick means twice as fast. Right: between 2.5 and 4 times as fast, because the time grows faster than the thickness. | sentences=5

table.name: E8-stiffer-is-not-better: Why a stiffer partner layer does not bend the strip more (the modulus ratio drops out)
table.fields: explanation=You might expect a much stiffer passive layer to push the strip into a tighter curl. It does not. The best possible curl is the same, 1.5 times the mismatch divided by the thickness, whatever the stiffness ratio, provided you adjust the thicknesses. The recipe is that the stiffer layer is made thinner, by the square root of the stiffness ratio; equivalently stiffness x thickness squared is equal in both layers. If you ignore the recipe you lose curl: with a 10 times stiffness gap and equal thicknesses you get only 66 percent of the maximum [calc]. Make one layer infinitely stiffer than the other and the strip does not bend at all. | everyday_comparison=A seesaw: a heavy child sits closer to the pivot so that weight times distance balances. | where_it_breaks=The seesaw is our own gloss on the rule 'stiffness x thickness squared equal': the rule comes from algebra (m squared x n = 1), not from the seesaw. When the layers are about equally thick, stiffness hardly matters (Reyssat: f changes by under 10 percent for stiffness ratios 0.3 to 3.5; we get 0.9 percent at equal thickness [calc]). | common_wrong_idea=Wrong: stiffer partner, more bend. Right: the match between thickness and stiffness sets the bend, and the ceiling does not depend on the stiffness ratio. | sentences=6

table.name: E9-liquid-matters: Why Elastic 50A drinks 39 percent isopropanol but under 1 percent water
table.fields: explanation=How much a plastic swells depends on the liquid as much as the plastic. In Formlabs' 24-hour soak test, Elastic 50A V2 gained 39.2 percent of its weight in isopropyl alcohol but only 0.7 percent in water, while Rigid 10K gained under 0.1 percent in both. The stiff resin has little room for any liquid, and the soft rubbery one lets some liquids in and others hardly at all. The practical lesson is that a water-driven design must be checked against every liquid the part meets, including a cleaning bath. The older Elastic 50A V1 took up 25.6 percent isopropanol and 2.3 percent water in the same test. | everyday_comparison=Salt dissolves in water but not in cooking oil: whether something gets in depends on the pairing. | where_it_breaks=The resin does not dissolve; the cured network swells and holds the liquid, so 'dissolving' is the wrong picture. The reason one liquid gets in and another does not is general chemistry, not shown in the sources I fetched. | common_wrong_idea=Wrong: if it ignores water it ignores every liquid. Right: water uptake and alcohol uptake are separate numbers. | sentences=5

recommendations: Always say 'mass percent in a 24 h cube test' when quoting a Formlabs water uptake, and never 'water uptake of Formlabs resins' as one figure: Flexible 80A V2 is +8 % in a day.

When explaining the ceiling to the architecture practice, show the 1863 formula (a = 1 + square) beside the Lean proof: a layperson can see that no choice beats 1.5, and credit Holstov 2015 for the numerical observation.
State the limits of Lean every time it is mentioned: it proves the maths of the model, not that a printed strip will behave.
Measure it: coupon strips of Rigid 10K and Flexible 80A V2 weighed and measured at 24 h, 1 week and equilibrium would turn every labelled estimate here (strain per percent mass, D) into data.

If a hands-on demo is wanted for visitors, use the paper-and-tape curl or a real pine cone in a bowl of water (cone closes, then reopens on drying) as the opening act before showing the printed sample.
